newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Tension grows in Armenia over contested vote.
newsitem.headline: Tension grows in Armenia over contested vote.

text.p: Elite commando troops took up positions around key buildings in the Armenian capital Yerevan on Tuesday as the country appeared bound for an acute political crisis over Sunday's presidential election.
More than 100 red-beret clad unarmed soldiers fanned out around the large brick parliament building and security was beefed up at President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's official residence.

A high fence separated the soldiers guarding the parliament from a crowd of at least 25,000 people, waving national flags and shouting anti-presidential slogans, clearly demonstrating support for Ter-Petrosyan's election rival Vazgen Manukyan.

Ter-Petrosyan on Monday proclaimed a "brilliant victory" in his quest for a second five-year term over former prime minister Manukyan, but his margin has been shrinking as late votes are counted in a contest marred by irregularities.
Around a dozen armed men reinforced guards at the presidential palace while soldiers armed with Kalashnikov rifles sealed off the television station.

The parliament houses the Central Elections Commission, which has been compiling votes from Sunday's contest. But commission officials mysteriously left in the mid-afternoon and stopped giving updates on vote totals.
A scheduled press briefing was also abruptly called off.
The last incomplete figures given at around midday by commission members showed Ter-Petrosyan with 51.99 percent of the vote to 41.16 for Manukyan.
The other two candidates who took part in the Sunday vote failed to win any substantial backing. Ter-Petrosyan needs more than 50 percent of the vote to avoid a second round runoff.
Armenian state radio later quoted the commission as saying Ter-Petrosyan's share of the vote had fallen to 48 percent after further counting, but this could not be confirmed.
"Everyone has left the building," said one of the soldiers guarding the parliament.

Manukyan, a 50-year old physicist, and his supporters have said the government rigged the vote in favour of Ter-Petrosyan. The former prime minister led 50,000 peaceful protesters through the streets of central Yerevan on Monday.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which has been coordinating 89 international observers, issued a preliminary report criticising "very serious" irregularities in voting procedures.

It detailed incidences of soldiers being ordered to vote for Ter-Petrosyan by their commanding officers, and said members of the armed forces and interior ministry had been present in many polling stations contrary to the law.

In one case the report said a group of people had cut off the power supply to one Yerevan polling station and then stolen a ballot box and papers. Observers said they had established the culprits were Ter-Petrosyan campaigners.
The report stopped short however of formally questioning the legitamacy of the election, saying the abuses "do not in themselves constitute a systematic attempt to deny the will of the people".
Some individual observers thought the report could have been far more forceful in detailing abuses.

"What most of us saw was definitely classifiable as systematic fraud on a massive scale. The vast majority of us are very unhappy with the report. We felt it tried to hard to avoid embarrassing the government," said one observer on condition of anonymity.
"I thought the report should have said specifically who committed the abuses. Most of the irreguarities we saw were being committed by Ter-Petrosyan's people," said another.
The contest between the two former close allies, both of whom played big roles in leading Armenia to independence from the Soviet union in 1991, had grown bitter before the vote.

Ter-Petrosyan, 51, launched blistering attacks in the closing hours of the campaign saying that a Manukyan presidency would bring "tyranny and chaos". Manukyan for his part hit back accusing the president of having mafia connections.
